topic: Law fact / myth-buster: a married, earning or separately living child, spouse or sibling is not automatically barred from motor accident compensation - all legal representatives can claim under Section 166 MV Act without proving dependency; dependency is decided case by case and affects share; married daughter treated as partially dependent, award enhanced by over Rs 12 lakh with 9% interest (United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Savita & Anr., 2026:DHC:9920, Justice Anish Dayal, Delhi HC, reported 12 Nov 2026)

slides.title: Married or earning? You can **still claim**
slides.subtitle: Being married, employed or living separately does **not** by itself shut a family member out of road accident compensation, says the Delhi High Court.
slides.cite: **United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Savita & Anr.** · 2026:DHC:9920 · Justice Anish Dayal · Delhi High Court · reported 12 Nov 2026

slides.label: The myth
slides.title: "Married daughter? **No claim**"
bullets: **Fact:** a married or earning child, spouse or sibling cannot be excluded **just because** they are married, employed or live apart.
Every **legal representative** of the person who died can file a claim under **Section 166** of the Motor Vehicles Act.
They do **not** first have to prove they were financially dependent.

slides.label: What happened
slides.title: Father and sister lost in **one accident**
bullets: A woman lost her father and her sister in a road accident in **2015**. She had married in 2002 and lived separately.
The tribunal treated her as a **non-dependent** and gave her only a reduced 'loss of estate' amount.
The insurer argued she was married and **not dependent** at all.

slides.label: The ruling
slides.title: Dependency is **not** a fixed box
bullets: Dependency must be judged on the **facts of each case**, not by rigid 'dependent / non-dependent' labels.
Indian families often share a **common family income**. A member living elsewhere may still draw support from it.
She was held **partly dependent**. Her award went up by over **Rs 12 lakh**, with 9% interest.
slides.note: **Law fact:** dependency still matters for the share. A fully dependent family member should get a **bigger share** than a partly dependent one.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: A right to claim, **not** a fixed amount
bullets: This does **not** mean every relative gets the same money. The tribunal decides the amount and each person's share.
'Legal representative', 'legal heir' and 'dependant' mean **different things** in law, the court said.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

caption:
Married, earning or living separately? You may still claim road accident compensation for a family member 🚗⚖️

Myth: "A married daughter, an earning spouse or a sibling who lives apart cannot claim anything." The Delhi High Court has said this is wrong. Such a family member cannot be excluded just because they are married, employed or live separately. Every legal representative of the deceased can file a claim under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act without first proving financial dependency.

The case: a woman lost her father and sister in a 2015 road accident. She had married years earlier and lived with her own family. The tribunal treated her as a non-dependent and gave her only a reduced amount, and the insurer argued she was not dependent at all. The High Court said dependency cannot be put into fixed boxes and must be judged on the facts. Indian families often share a common family income, and a member living elsewhere may still draw support from it.

The court held she was partly dependent and raised her compensation by over Rs 12 lakh, with 9% interest. Remember, dependency still affects the share: a fully dependent member should get more than a partly dependent one, and the tribunal decides the amount in each case.

Case: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Savita & Anr., 2026:DHC:9920
Bench: Justice Anish Dayal, Delhi High Court (reported 12 Nov 2026)
